clue.text: Expression unravels when spoken?

indicators.note: something spoken is heard rather than read, so the sound counts and not the spelling

blocks.note: a rope that unravels frays at the end

explanation.surface: A puzzled remark that some saying comes apart as soon as anyone utters it.
explanation.walkthrough: FRAYS and PHRASE sound identical, so the verb for coming apart turns into a word for a form of words.
explanation.definitionFit: A phrase is a short group of words, so it is a synonym for an expression or saying.

clue.text: Clerical history exam

blocks.note: history is what lies in the past
an oral is a spoken examination

explanation.surface: It reads like a church-history paper sat by trainee clergy.
explanation.walkthrough: The three words look like one subject heading; the first is the definition and the other two are consecutive pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Pastoral describes the work of a pastor or priest caring for a congregation, so it relates closely to clergy.

clue.text: Francophiles’ yen to develop their own territory?

indicators.note: developing something changes its shape, so these letters are rebuilt into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Lovers of all things French long to cultivate a land of their own.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Yen' looks like a longing or a currency, but here it is just three letters of fodder; 'their' refers back to France, which owns the territory.
explanation.definitionFit: French Polynesia is an overseas collectivity governed by France in the South Pacific, so it is a territory belonging to the French.

clue.text: Apparently having missed par, going round in high numbers

indicators.note: to miss something is to go without it, so those letters are absent from the word
letters that go round are moved about, so the remainder is rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written, to be removed

explanation.surface: A golfer who failed to make par and went round with a big score.
explanation.walkthrough: Removing the letters P, A, R from the first word leaves APENTLY, and shifting the L gives the answer. Golf terms 'par' and 'going round' are pure disguise.
explanation.definitionFit: Aplenty is an adverb meaning in abundance or in large quantities, matching the idea of high numbers.

clue.text: Things are more complicated as spadework gets tougher?

blocks.note: first meaning: the familiar remark when a situation grows more intricate
second meaning, taken literally: a patch of garden soil becoming denser to dig

explanation.surface: A gardener finds digging harder as the work goes on, and everything gets more complicated.
explanation.walkthrough: The second half reads the idiom literally: a plot is a piece of ground, and when it thickens the spade has a harder job.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom announces that a story or situation is getting more intricate and mysterious, which is what more complicated things are.

clue.text: Pressure someone initially put on lock

indicators.note: initially means at the start, so only the opening letter is kept
putting one thing on another places them together, so one piece is attached to the other

blocks.note: the opening letter of the word
a tress is a lock of hair

explanation.surface: Somebody at first applies force to a lock, like a burglar leaning on a door.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lock' suggests a door fastening, but it is a lock of hair. In a down clue, 'put on' places the first piece on top of the second.
explanation.definitionFit: Stress and pressure are synonyms, both meaning a force or strain applied to something or someone.

clue.text: Partly scoop up some litter

definitions.note: a litter is a whole brood; the answer is its members

indicators.note: partly means only in part, so the letters sit across the following words

blocks.note: the letters run across the end of the first word, the second word and the start of the third

explanation.surface: An instruction to clear away some rubbish from the street.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Litter' suggests rubbish to scoop up, but it means the young born together to a dog. 'Some' serves both as part of the hidden letters and to qualify the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Young dogs are born several at a time, and a group born together is called a litter.

clue.text: Stop question and answer

blocks.note: who is a question word
A is the standard abbreviation for answer

explanation.surface: Someone halts a quiz session of question and answer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Question and answer' looks like a fixed phrase, but each word gives its own piece.
explanation.definitionFit: Whoa is the call used to make a horse halt, and is used generally as a command to wait or cease.

clue.text: Hip-hop hit

blocks.note: first meaning: the rhythmic spoken style of music
second meaning: a sharp knock or blow

explanation.walkthrough: It reads like a chart-topping song; the two words are separate meanings of one short word.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names a music genre closely tied to hip-hop and also a quick sharp blow, as on a door.

clue.text: Attractive though withdrawn, often bubbly thing?

indicators.note: something withdrawn is pulled back, so this word runs backwards

blocks.note: hot is slang for sexy or attractive
but and though both introduce a contrast

explanation.surface: A description of a good-looking but shy person who is usually lively and effervescent.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface sounds like a personality, attractive yet reserved, but bubbly; 'withdrawn' works on the second piece only.
explanation.definitionFit: A hot tub is a heated outdoor bath whose water jets usually churn up bubbles.

clue.text: Bird hurting where wings clipped

indicators.note: the wings of a word are its two ends, and clipping them trims both away

blocks.note: smarting means stinging or hurting

explanation.surface: A bird is in pain because its wings have been clipped.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wings' sounds part of the bird picture, but means the outer letters of the word for hurting.
explanation.definitionFit: The martin is a small swallow-like bird, such as the house martin, so it is an example of a bird.

clue.text: Teas oddly ignored, media types love coffee

indicators.note: ignoring the odd-numbered positions keeps only the even ones

blocks.note: the second and fourth letters
the press is journalists collectively
love is zero in tennis, a round O

explanation.surface: Journalists turn their noses up at tea but adore coffee.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Love' looks like the verb of the surface; it is the zero score in tennis.
explanation.definitionFit: Espresso is a strong coffee made by forcing steam through ground beans, so it is a specific kind of coffee.

clue.text: Rule the roost — taking strides to do it?

blocks.note: first meaning: be the dominant one in a household
second meaning, literal: strides is British slang for a pair of legwear

explanation.surface: Someone takes big steps to become the boss of the household.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Strides' suggests walking purposefully, but in British slang strides are trousers, so the second half reads the idiom literally.
explanation.definitionFit: To be the person in charge of a household is an idiomatic sense of the phrase, just as ruling the roost is.

clue.text: Newspaper in stew when not published!

indicators.note: 'not' removes something, so the following word's letters are taken away

blocks.note: a ragout is a highly seasoned French stew
a book that is published is out

explanation.surface: A newspaper is in a stew, flustered, because it did not get printed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In a stew' looks like the idiom for agitation, but 'in' only links the definition to the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Rag is a dismissive informal word for a newspaper, especially a low-quality one.

clue.text: Believe in drink?

blocks.note: first meaning: accept a story without question
second meaning: take liquid down the throat

explanation.walkthrough: 'Believe in' reads as one phrase, but 'in' just joins two separate meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: One verb covers both senses: to gulp liquid down and, informally, to accept a claim credulously.

clue.text: Series of hostile actions friendly? Not entirely!

indicators.note: not entirely means not complete, so the word loses its final letter

blocks.note: warm means friendly and welcoming

explanation.surface: Someone queries whether a run of aggressive acts could be called friendly.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark makes 'friendly' seem a sarcastic comment on the hostilities; it is the source word.
explanation.definitionFit: A war is a prolonged state of armed conflict, made up of a sequence of hostile acts.

clue.text: Space to get angry after ending of negotiations

indicators.note: the ending of a word is its final letter, so only that is kept
after signals that the preceding pieces follow the later one in the answer

blocks.note: the final letter of the word
taken as written
to rage is to be furious

explanation.surface: Someone loses their temper once talks finally collapse and asks for room.
explanation.walkthrough: 'To' looks like part of the infinitive 'to get angry', but it supplies its own two letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Storage means room set aside for keeping things, so it is a sense of space as in a cupboard or loft.

clue.text: Bell’s taken on cricket shot, opener

blocks.note: to bell is to ring, and a bell's sound is a ring
a pull is a cricket stroke hitting a short ball to the leg side

explanation.surface: England batter Ian Bell plays a cricket stroke as an opening batsman.
explanation.walkthrough: Bell suggests the cricketer Ian Bell and 'opener' an opening batter, but both are disguises; in a down clue 'taken on' sets the first piece above the second.
explanation.definitionFit: A ring pull is the tab on a drinks can that you lift to open it, so it serves as an opener.

clue.text: Where spinner resides online?

blocks.note: surface reading: the internet home of a spin doctor or a spin bowler
setter's reading: a spider spins, and it lives on the threads it weaves

explanation.walkthrough: 'Online' pushes the reader to the internet, which is half right; the spinner is a spider whose home is its silken net.
explanation.definitionFit: A website is a location on the internet, and read as two words it is the place where a spider's web sits.

clue.text: Be with ministers, pray desperately for Church governance

indicators.note: acting desperately means wildly and without order, so the letters are scrambled

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Join the clergy and plead fervently for church rule by elders.
explanation.walkthrough: The ecclesiastical surface makes the anagram fodder blend in with the definition; 'with' simply joins the first two pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Presbyterianism is a system of running a church through elected elders rather than bishops, so it is a form of ecclesiastical government.

clue.text: Priest played in band

indicators.note: something played with is moved about, so the letters change their order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A vicar performed as a member of a musical group.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Band' looks like a music group, but it means a strip of colour.
explanation.definitionFit: A stripe is a long narrow strip of colour, which is one sense of the noun band.

clue.text: Solver thus excited about last two in puzzle …

indicators.note: excited letters are stirred up, so they come out in a new order
the last two of a word are its final pair of letters, and only those are kept
about means around, so one piece surrounds another

blocks.note: taken as written
the final pair of letters

explanation.surface: A crossword solver gets thrilled on reaching the final two clues, which run on into the next one.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis is surface only: it makes the two clues read as a single sentence about finishing a puzzle.
explanation.definitionFit: A sleuth is a detective, someone who works out mysteries, which is a fair description of a person who solves things.

clue.text: Minimum on head, still bald!

indicators.note: on links two things placed together, so one piece joins the other

blocks.note: by association: what grows on a head
less means a smaller amount, the direction of the minimum

explanation.surface: Even with the smallest amount of growth on top, a man is still bald.
explanation.walkthrough: The pieces come out in reverse clue order: the thing on the head first, then the word for a smaller amount.
explanation.definitionFit: Hairless and bald both describe a scalp or body with no hair growing on it, so they are synonyms.

clue.text: … get rid of last of all — and jump!

indicators.note: the last of a word is its final letter, so only that one is kept

blocks.note: to axe is to cut or get rid of
the final letter of the word

explanation.surface: Continuing the previous clue, the solver throws everything away and leaps.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Last of all' sounds like 'finally', but it is the final letter of the word 'all'.
explanation.definitionFit: An axel is a figure-skating leap with a forward take-off and extra half rotation, so it is a kind of jump.

clue.text: Fish, one in the Land of Nod?

definitions.text: one in the Land of Nod

blocks.note: first meaning: a split, salted and smoked herring

blocks.clueFragment: one in the Land of Nod
blocks.note: second meaning: someone who kips, British slang for sleeping

explanation.walkthrough: The Land of Nod is a playful name for sleep, and a kip is British slang for a nap, so a sleeper is one who kips.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is a smoked herring eaten at breakfast and, whimsically, a person asleep or taking a nap.

clue.text: Location of Oracle where I held out to maintain power

indicators.note: out can mean wrong or disordered, so the letters before it are rearranged
to maintain is to hold, so one piece keeps another inside it

blocks.note: taken as written
P is the standard abbreviation for power

explanation.surface: A shrine where a seer refused to give way so as to keep hold of power.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Held out' reads as resisted, but 'out' scrambles the two words before it into the Indian capital, which then holds the power abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: The ancient Greek sanctuary of Apollo was home to the famous oracle, the Pythia, who gave prophecies there.

clue.text: Metal prong shortened

indicators.note: a shortened word is cut down, losing its final letter

blocks.note: a tine is a prong of a fork or antler

explanation.surface: A metal spike, perhaps on a fork, has been cut down.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a physical prong being trimmed; the trimming is done to the word.
explanation.definitionFit: Tin is a soft silvery chemical element, so it is an example of a metal.

clue.text: Stuck in mail, a telegram yet to arrive

indicators.note: something stuck in is lodged inside, so the letters sit within the following words

blocks.note: the letters run from the end of the first word across to the start of the third

explanation.surface: A telegram is held up in the post and has not been delivered.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is about delayed post, so the hidden answer sits right in the scene.
explanation.definitionFit: Late describes something that has not appeared by the expected time, so it fits something still awaited.
